A century of yearly inflation, and why the averages need care

A long-term plan usually needs one inflation figure: 2% or 2.5% a year is common, and the Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation at the 2% midpoint of a 1% to 3% target range. That target is a policy aim, and the Bank says it was adopted with the Government of Canada only in 1991. A saver who is 35 today is planning across 30 years or more, and over a span that long the average result has varied far more than the year-to-year noise suggests.

A single inflation assumption hides how differently decades have turned out. Using Statistics Canada’s CPI back to 1914, see what a dollar kept over every overlapping 10, 20 or 30-year window, how often prices rose faster than a planning assumption, and how often a steady return after fees and tax kept up.

Above zero, the loan left the household with more after tax by that year than investing in your own name. The rate is fixed for the life of the loan, so a loan made at 1% in 2021 or early 2022 still costs 1%, while one made in early 2024 locked in 6%. At your inputs the loan breaks even at about 4.41%. The interest costs the household the gap between your two tax rates each year, so it pays only when the fund’s income and growth taxed at the lower rate save more than that.

Across 92 overlapping 20-year windows of Canadian CPI, the median rise in prices was 2.82% a year. The fastest was 1971–1991 at 7.13% a year, when a dollar kept 25 cents of its buying power, so $50,000 of today’s spending would need $198,164; at your 2.5% assumption it needs $81,931. 55% of windows ran hotter than your assumption. A steady 4.00% a year after fees and tax would have kept purchasing power in 75% of them. History is a range of past outcomes, not a forecast.

Across the 92 overlapping 20-year windows from 1914–1934 to 2005–2025, Canadian prices rose by a median of 2.82% a year, but the range ran from prices falling 1.75% a year (1920–1940) to rising 7.13% a year (1971–1991), when a dollar kept only about a quarter of its buying power. A goal costing CAD 50,000 today needs about CAD 81,900 in 20 years at 2.5% inflation, and about CAD 198,200 if prices rose as they did over 1971–1991. A steady 4% a year after fees and tax kept purchasing power in 75% of the 20-year windows and 62% of the 30-year windows. History shows the spread a plan should allow for; it does not say which part of it comes next.

Against that, the fund’s yearly payouts and its eventual gain are taxed at 25% instead of 48%. With a 6% return of which 2.5% is paid out each year, the loan leaves the household about CAD 8,173 ahead after tax at year 15, counting the after-tax interest you reinvest in your own name. The break-even prescribed rate is about 4.41%. For someone saving from each paycheque, inflation acts on both sides of the plan. A fixed monthly contribution shrinks in real terms if it is never raised, while pay has, over long periods, tended to rise with prices, though not in every year or for every worker. Raising contributions once a year by the CPI keeps the real amount saved roughly level; the indexed contributions guide shows the difference over a career. That is a different situation from a lump sum already saved, where the question is how the existing balance is invested and in which account, not how much new money to add.

How often history ran hotter than your assumption

If you give money to a spouse or common-law partner who invests it in a non-registered fund, the Income Tax Act attributes the income and capital gains back to you, so the household pays tax at your rate as before. Money your spouse puts in their own TFSA is excepted. A loan at the prescribed rate, 3% for loans made in the fourth quarter of 2026, also avoids attribution if the interest for each year is paid by 30 January of the next year. With CAD 100,000, a 6% return of which 2.5% is paid out yearly, and tax rates of 48% and 25%, the loan leaves the household about CAD 8,200 ahead after tax over 15 years, and using CAD 30,000 of TFSA room first adds about CAD 14,300 more. With no yearly payouts, or a much smaller rate gap, the interest can cost more than it saves.

Saving from pay through a high-inflation decade

Section 74.1 of the Income Tax Act says that when an individual transfers or lends property to a spouse or common-law partner, income or loss from that property, or from property substituted for it, is deemed to be the individual’s and not the spouse’s, for as long as both are resident in Canada and remain a couple; section 74.2 does the same for capital gains and losses. So a gift that your spouse invests in a non-registered fund is still taxed at your rate. In the calculator, the first bar therefore stands for both investing in your own name and gifting the money for a taxable account.

Section 74.5(2) switches the attribution rules off for income and gains from lent property in a year if three conditions hold: interest is charged at no less than the lesser of the prescribed rate in effect when the loan was made and an arm’s-length rate; the interest for that year is paid no later than 30 days after the year ends; and the interest for every earlier year was paid on time too. In practice that means paying each year’s interest by 30 January. Missing one payment means attribution applies for that year and every later year of the loan.
Separation, death, a change of residence or a change in the prescribed-rate rules would change the result; the calculator assumes none.

Tax matters in the same way. Interest earned outside a registered account is taxed every year on its full nominal amount, including the part that only replaces lost buying power; at a 40% rate, 4% interest leaves 2.4%. CRA says that interest, dividends and capital gains earned in a TFSA are generally tax-free, even when withdrawn, so the account can matter as much as the investment. The tax treatment comes from the account, not from the fund itself: the same balanced fund is taxed differently in a TFSA, an RRSP and a non-registered account, as the guide to tax on inflation gains shows.
The CPI is an average basket. Your own costs, such as rent, food or care, can rise faster or slower; the personal inflation guide shows how to weigh them.

The calculator taxes payouts as ordinary income, which suits interest-paying bond funds and overstates the tax on funds that pay eligible dividends or capital gains distributions; the fund income guide compares those types. CRA treats reinvested distributions as taxable in the year paid and adds them to the cost base. Lower returns also weaken the case: at 3% a year the default loan is about CAD 1,000 behind. None of these returns is assured, and a balanced fund can lose value in a year when the interest is still due.

The first chart compares each calendar year’s average CPI with the year before. Prices rose 17.96% in 1917 and fell 12.11% in 1921; they fell in ten years in all, the last in 1953. Every year from 1973 to 1982 was above 7%. More recently, inflation was 6.80% in 2022 and 2.07% in 2025, and the index for September 2026 was 3.09% above September 2025.

The grid uses constant returns because they make the comparison exact, not because any investment delivers one. A balanced fund holds stocks and bonds, and its return varies widely from year to year, with losses in some years. High-inflation periods were often hard on both parts at once: rising interest rates push bond prices down, and the guide to years when stocks and bonds fall together uses 2022 as an example. Equities have historically offered more growth potential over long periods than cash, but with larger declines, and no return or recovery by a particular date is assured.

The heatmap takes a steady yearly return, removes the fee you enter, taxes what is left at the rate you enter, and counts the share of past windows in which it at least matched the rise in prices. A steady 4% with no fee or tax kept purchasing power in 75% of the 20-year windows and 62% of the 30-year windows; 6% kept up in every 30 and 40-year window. A 1.5% fee turns that 4% into 2.5%, which kept up over 20 years in fewer than half of the windows.

The heatmap varies your spouse’s marginal rate and the prescribed rate while keeping you at 48%. A spouse with no income tax and a 1% loan gives the largest benefit; with a spouse at 40% the 3% loan is about CAD 2,700 ahead and at 5% it is behind. Where the two rates are close, a loan adds paperwork and a yearly deadline for little or no gain. Combining TFSA gifts first with a loan for the rest gave the highest after-tax value in the default case, about CAD 206,300 after 15 years against CAD 183,900 in your own name.
The loan works on income paid out each year more than on deferred growth

The practical use is a stress test. A goal costing CAD 50,000 in today’s dollars needs about CAD 81,900 in 20 years at 2.5% a year, about CAD 87,200 at the 2.82% median and about CAD 198,200 if prices rose as they did from 1971 to 1991. A plan does not have to be built on the worst window, but it helps to know what a higher path would require: more saving, a later date, a smaller goal or a mix with more growth potential and more risk. The price-level guide shows why prices do not fall back after a burst of inflation slows.
The rate gap and the prescribed rate decide most of it

The rate is fixed when the loan is made and is not reset as CRA’s rate changes. The Income Tax Regulations set each quarter’s rate as the average 3-month treasury bill yield at the auctions held in the first month of the previous quarter, rounded up to the next whole percent. The first chart shows the result: 1% in late 2021 and the first half of 2022, a peak of 6% in the first half of 2024, and 3% since July 2025, including October to December 2026. A loan made at 1% in 2021 still costs 1% today; one made in early 2024 still costs 6%.

The regulation sets each quarter’s rate from the average 3-month treasury bill yield at auctions in the first month of the previous quarter, rounded up to the next whole percent. The dashed line is the Bank of Canada’s monthly series for that month, a close but not identical measure: rounding it up matches CRA’s rate in 19 of the 21 quarters, but for the second quarters of 2024 and 2025 it gives one point less than CRA set (4.94% against 6%, and 2.89% against 4%), because the regulation averages that month’s auctions rather than taking one reading. The rate was 1% in late 2021 and the first half of 2022, peaked at 6% in the first half of 2024 and has been 3% since July 2025, including the fourth quarter of 2026. A loan keeps the rate in effect on the day it is made.
The returns in the grid are constant by construction, with the fee and tax applied every year. Real returns vary, taxes depend on the account and the type of income, and fees change.
The same fund, two tax rates in one household

The saving comes mainly from yearly taxable payouts, which is why the type of fund matters. If the fund paid out nothing and all of the 6% were deferred growth, the household would be about CAD 1,300 behind with the loan after 15 years at 3%: the interest costs money every year, while the tax saving on a deferred gain arrives only when it is sold and is halved by the 50% inclusion rate. With 4% paid out each year, the loan is about CAD 12,600 ahead and breaks even at a prescribed rate of about 5.2%.

The second chart divides the average index in the first year of each window by the average in its last year. With 20-year windows, the median result was inflation of 2.82% a year, close to many planning assumptions. But the worst window, 1971 to 1991, averaged 7.13% a year: CAD 1 at the start could buy only what CAD 0.25 had bought. In the best, 1920 to 1940, prices fell 1.75% a year and a dollar bought more at the end than at the start. Seven of the 92 windows ended with prices lower than they began, and all of them started between 1917 and 1923.

The statutory conditions are only part of it. Tax practitioners commonly recommend a written loan agreement with the amount, rate and date, the loan going to an account in your spouse’s name, and interest paid each January from your spouse’s own money with a record such as a bank transfer, so the arrangement can be shown to be what it says it is. If interest is paid by selling fund units, the sale can realize gains, as the calculator assumes. Separate rules apply to loans to minors, to trusts and to other related adults, including section 56(4.1) on low-interest loans, which this guide does not cover. Because missing a 30 January payment cannot be fixed afterwards, a tax professional can help set it up.

The third chart counts the windows by their average inflation. With the default 2.5% assumption, 55% of the 20-year windows ran above it. That does not mean a 55% chance of the next 20 years doing so: the record includes two world wars, the Depression and the oil shocks, and the inflation-targeting era since the 1990s has been calmer. Set the first year to 1991 and the windows reflect only that era, which leaves far fewer of them to judge by.

There are exceptions. Section 74.5(12) says the attribution rules do not apply to property your spouse holds in their own TFSA or FHSA, as long as the contribution does not create an excess amount in that account, and a premium you pay to a spousal RRSP and deduct is also excluded. Giving your spouse money to fill their unused TFSA room is therefore usually the first and simplest step: CRA says income and gains earned in a TFSA are generally tax-free, even when withdrawn. The over-contribution tax still applies, so check their room first; the TFSA excess guide explains it.

These are dated observations, with two cautions. The basket and the methods behind the CPI have changed many times since 1914, so the early figures describe a different set of purchases from today’s. And an annual average smooths the months: a year-over-year change in a single month, the figure usually quoted in the news, can differ from the change in the annual average. The CPI measurement guide covers those differences.

This guide uses Statistics Canada’s Consumer Price Index from January 1914 to look at every overlapping stretch of years: 1914 to 1934, 1915 to 1935, and so on up to 2005 to 2025. For each one it asks how much a dollar could still buy at the end. The inflation basics guide explains how a constant rate compounds; this one shows how far real decades have strayed from any constant rate.

This is a decision about who owns an existing lump sum. Saving from each paycheque is a separate question: a lower earner can usually invest their own pay in their own name, and new contributions can be directed to the lower earner’s TFSA. If the higher earner pays more of the household bills so the lower earner can invest their own earnings, that is a different arrangement from a gift or loan of capital.

What the history does support is that money expected to be spent decades from now has to be judged in real terms. Cash and short-term deposits protect the nominal amount, which matters for money needed soon, but over long windows they have often lost purchasing power after tax. Holding a growth-oriented share of a long-term plan is one response to that, with risk that has to suit the person and the time available; the balanced-fund crash and inflation guide sets those risks side by side.

When one partner pays tax at a much higher rate than the other, investment income looks cheaper in the lower earner’s hands. A balanced fund held outside a registered account pays out interest, dividends and capital gains each year, and every dollar of that taxed at 25% instead of 48% leaves more to compound. The question is how to get the money there legally. This guide compares three routes for savings beyond each partner’s own RRSP and TFSA: investing in your own name, giving the money to your spouse, and lending it at the prescribed rate. It assumes both partners have already used the room in their own accounts; the account decides the tax, and the fund inside it is the same.
